analysis.one_liner: Restricts FBI searches of Americans' communications while extending the Section 702 surveillance program.
analysis.headline: The House Intelligence Committee cleared it on a bipartisan voice vote in December 2023, but the full House never voted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reauthorize Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the program that lets the government collect communications of foreigners abroad that incidentally sweep in Americans' calls and emails. It would place new limits on how the FBI can search that trove of Americans' information: barring searches made solely to find evidence of a crime, requiring supervisor approval before querying an American's name, mandating audits, and notifying Congress when a member of Congress is queried. At the same time, it would extend the surveillance program for years, add drug trafficking to the definition of foreign intelligence, and expand the list of companies required to help the government conduct surveillance.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans would get the most direct benefit: new limits on warrantless FBI searches of their communications, mandatory audits of those searches, and a court-appointed lawyer to challenge the government's surveillance applications when an American is targeted. The intelligence agencies would also benefit from a guaranteed multi-year extension of the program plus new authority to collect on international drug trafficking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans whose data the FBI queries

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit FBI queries of Section 702 data that are solely designed to find and extract evidence of a crime, except when there is a reasonable belief a query could help address a threat to life or serious bodily harm [S2].

It would require FBI personnel to obtain supervisor or attorney approval before running a search using an American's name or other identifying information, and would ban political appointees from the approval process [S2].
It would bar the FBI from ingesting unminimized 702 data into its repositories unless the target is relevant to an existing, predicated full national security investigation [S2].
It would require the FBI Director to notify congressional leadership and the member involved whenever a query uses the name or personal information of a Member of Congress [S2].

It would mandate Justice Department audits of FBI queries of Americans' information and require annual reports on the number of such queries, made publicly available after declassification review [S2].
It would require the surveillance court to appoint counsel to scrutinize applications targeting United States persons and to appoint an amicus to review the annual Section 702 certifications [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The FBI and the wider intelligence community would give up operational flexibility and face audits, reporting, and personnel accountability for noncompliant queries. Tech and telecom companies would bear expanded obligations to help the government conduct surveillance under a broadened definition of 'electronic communication service provider.' And the multi-year extension would lock in a surveillance program that sweeps in Americans' communications with no individual warrant.

drawbacks.text: The bill would extend the Section 702 program for years (Sec. 511, 'Extension of certain authorities; sunset') while adding drug trafficking to the definition of foreign intelligence and broadening the 'electronic communication service provider' definition so more companies can be compelled to assist surveillance [S2].

Its query limits contain large exceptions: a 'threat to life or serious bodily harm' carve-out, an exception for litigation and discovery purposes, and a provision letting the surveillance court waive many requirements entirely if it finds alternative measures sufficient [S2].

It would raise criminal penalties for unauthorized disclosures to up to 10 years and create a new 8-year felony for disclosing classified information containing the contents of incidentally collected Americans' communications, provisions that could reach more kinds of disclosures than current law [S2].

The bill does not include a warrant requirement, which critics in both parties argued was the minimum needed before reauthorizing a program that collects Americans' communications; the FBI and the program's supporters opposed a warrant requirement on operational grounds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a compromise built to keep the 702 program alive while addressing its best-documented abuse: FBI searches of Americans' data. The query restrictions, audits, and court safeguards are real, but they are paired with a multi-year reauthorization, a wider surveillance mandate, and broad waivers, so the deal trades concrete privacy limits for locking in the program's core collection. Critics who wanted a judge's warrant before the FBI searches an American's data would say the reforms fall short of the problem.

outcome.mechanism: The Intelligence Committee cleared it, but the House rejected the procedural rule for taking the bill up in April 2024, so it never got a floor vote, and leadership instead passed a different reauthorization from the Senate.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Turner introduced the bill on December 6, 2023 with Rep. Jim Himes; it was referred to the Judiciary and Intelligence Committees [S4].
The House Intelligence Committee held a markup on December 7, ordered the bill reported by voice vote, and formally reported it on December 8 as H. Rept. 118-302, Part I [S4].
The full House never voted on the bill: the action record shows no floor action after the committee report, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The FBI and intelligence agencies kept operating under the existing law, and leadership salvaged a five-year reauthorization of 702 through a different bill that spring, so the agencies came out ahead while this bill's query restrictions never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies; a different reauthorization passed instead

sides.party_line_note: The Intelligence Committee cleared the bill on a bipartisan voice vote under a Republican chair and Democratic ranking member, but the opposition that killed it on the floor came from both parties, including Republicans who wanted a warrant requirement and Democrats who wanted stronger privacy protections.

industries.note: The FBI would lose the ability to freely search 702 data for ordinary criminal evidence and would face audits and personnel accountability, but it gains a guaranteed multi-year reauthorization of the program and new counternarcotics collection authority. For the public, the same trade cuts both ways: fewer warrantless searches of Americans, but a longer life for mass collection.

The bill broadens the definition of 'electronic communication service provider' to include equipment that may be used to transmit or store communications, pulling more companies into mandatory assistance with government surveillance. That expands the private infrastructure used to collect communications, including those of the providers' own users.
